title: A2.1 Origins of cells · Lesson 1 (HL): Early Earth, what counts as alive, and the problem of the first cell
summary: IB DP Biology · A2.1 Origins of cells

1: There was no free oxygen [1], and plentiful energy from UV light (no ozone) and lightning drove reactions [1]; today oxygen would oxidise/break down the compounds and organisms would consume them [1].
2: Bacterium and yeast live; virus and crystal do not.
Viruses have no metabolism of their own (no ribosomes or cytoplasm) [1] and can only reproduce inside a host cell [1].
3: Cells are highly complex [1]; today they arise only by division of pre-existing cells [1]; the first cell required catalysis, self-replication, self-assembly and compartmentalization all to arise from non-living chemistry [1].
4: Yes: a dormant seed has very low metabolism but still carries out respiration slowly, maintains its cells and can grow and reproduce when conditions allow; it is a self-sustaining living system in a resting state.
5: No free oxygen and therefore no ozone layer [1]; high concentrations of CO₂ and methane [1]; high temperatures, intense UV light and lightning provided energy for reactions [1].
6: They lack their own metabolism and can reproduce only inside host cells.

title: A2.1 Origins of cells · Lesson 2 (HL): Miller–Urey, protocells and the RNA world
summary: IB DP Biology · A2.1 Origins of cells

1: It showed amino acids can form [1] from simple inorganic molecules with an energy source such as sparks [1]; but the gases used may not represent the early atmosphere, which was probably less reducing [1]; and it produced monomers, not polymers, nucleotides or cells [1].
2: A membrane separates internal chemistry from the outside [1], so molecules can be concentrated and reactions kept together, making the inside different from the environment [1].
3: RNA can store genetic information in its base sequence [1], be replicated by complementary base pairing [1], and act as a catalyst (ribozyme) [1].
4: Ocean: flask of boiling water; atmosphere: flask containing CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour; lightning: electrodes producing sparks; rain: the condenser cooling the gases back into liquid.
5: Some RNA molecules act as catalysts (ribozymes) [1]; ribosomal RNA in today’s ribosomes catalyses peptide bond formation, and RNA can store and replicate information [1].
6: Amino acids and other carbon compounds from simple inorganic gases with electric sparks.

title: A2.1 Origins of cells · Lesson 3 (HL): LUCA: evidence, dating and hydrothermal vents
summary: IB DP Biology · A2.1 Origins of cells

1: All organisms use the same genetic code [1]; hundreds of genes are shared across all domains [1]; all use the same biochemistry, e.g. DNA, ATP and the same 20 amino acids [1].
2: Stromatolites: fossils; carbon-12: isotope ratios; sequences: molecular clock.
3: Fossilised microbes have been found in ancient hydrothermal vent precipitates [1]; genomic analysis of conserved sequences predicts LUCA’s genes [1], which suit a vent environment: heat tolerance, use of H₂ and CO₂, iron–sulfur proteins [1].
4: Strength: vents supply energy, minerals and protection, and LUCA’s predicted genes fit vent life. Weakness: ancient fossils are disputed and high temperature and dilution in the ocean make polymerisation of RNA difficult; land ponds with wet–dry cycles may concentrate molecules better.
5: Fossils such as stromatolites [1], dated by radiometric dating, and isotope ratios in ancient rocks [1]; and molecular clock estimates from sequence differences between organisms [1].

title: A3.1 Diversity of organisms · Lesson 1: Variation, species and naming organisms
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.1 Diversity of organisms

tips: Think of a scientist in Japan and one in Kenya.

1: Vary: height, eye colour, blood group, fingerprints, voice. Same: e.g. 46 chromosomes, a backbone, bipedal walking — traits shared by all humans.
2: Homo sapiens and Vachellia tortilis are correct; “Homo Sapiens” has a capital S; loxodonta needs a capital L.
It is international, used by scientists in all languages [1]; each name is unique and unambiguous, and the genus shows which species are related [1].
3: They can interbreed but produce mules [1], which are infertile, so they do not meet the biological species definition of producing fertile offspring [1].
Only the forest birds; fossils, asexual bacteria and isolated populations cannot be tested.
4: Speciation happens gradually as populations diverge [1], so there is no clear point at which they become separate species; the decision is somewhat arbitrary [1].
5: A species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring [1]; it cannot be applied to fossils or asexually reproducing organisms [1]; some distinct species hybridise fertilely, and geographically isolated populations cannot be tested [1].
6: Genus with a capital initial, species name in lower case, both in italics (underlined if handwritten).

title: A3.1 Diversity of organisms · Lesson 2: Chromosome numbers, karyotypes and human chromosome 2
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.1 Diversity of organisms

tips: Three lines of evidence, then a judgement.

1: Body cells and zygotes are diploid (46); gametes haploid (23).
2: Chromosomes are arranged in homologous pairs [1], in order of decreasing length [1], matched by centromere position and banding pattern [1].
Sex and trisomy are visible; single-gene traits and base mutations are not.
3: Its banding pattern matches two chimpanzee chromosomes end to end [1]; telomere sequences are found in the middle of chromosome 2 [1]; there is a remnant second centromere [1]; together these consistently support the hypothesis, although the fusion itself was not observed [1].
4: The common ancestor probably had 48 chromosomes [1]; two chromosomes fused in the human lineage after it diverged from chimpanzees, giving 46 [1].
5: To determine biological sex from the sex chromosomes [1]; to diagnose chromosome abnormalities such as trisomy 21 [1].

title: A3.1 Diversity of organisms · Lesson 3: Genomes: unity, diversity, size and sequencing
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.1 Diversity of organisms

1: Members of a species share most of their genome/the same genes [1], but differ at some positions such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms, giving diversity [1].
2: SNPs and 0.1% differences are within species; large size differences are between species.
3: Humans (3 100 Mb) have a larger genome than yeast or fruit flies, which fits the claim [1]; but the marbled lungfish and Paris japonica have genomes over 40 times larger than humans [1]; so genome size does not correlate with complexity, largely because of non-coding DNA [1].
4: Evolution research and variant tracking are current; routine personalised prescribing for all is a future use.
A patient’s own genome is sequenced to identify relevant alleles/mutations [1], so drugs, doses or preventive measures can be chosen to suit that individual [1].
5: Within a species genomes are very similar, differing at SNPs (about 0.1% in humans) [1]; between species differences are much larger [1], in both base sequence and overall genome size [1].
6: A single-nucleotide polymorphism: a position in the genome where a single base differs between individuals of a species.

title: A3.1 Diversity of organisms · Lesson 4 (HL): Species in practice: asexual organisms, chromosome number, keys and eDNA
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.1 Diversity of organisms

1: Bacteria reproduce asexually, so interbreeding cannot be tested [1]; they exchange genes by horizontal gene transfer, even between different species [1].
2: A mule inherits 32 horse and 31 donkey chromosomes, 63 in total [1]; these cannot pair as homologues [1], so meiosis fails and viable gametes are not produced [1].
3: Example: 1a Leaves compound → 2; 1b Leaves simple → 3. 2a Thorns present → Vachellia tortilis; 2b No thorns → Jacaranda mimosifolia. 3a Leaf margin toothed → 4; 3b Leaf margin smooth → Ficus benjamina. 4a Leaves opposite → Lantana camara; 4b Leaves alternate → Hibiscus rosa-sinensis. Each couplet uses observable contrasting features.
Counts and leaf arrangement are good; vague size and behaviour are poor.
4: A water or soil sample containing DNA shed by organisms is collected [1]; barcode regions are amplified by PCR and sequenced [1]; sequences are compared with a reference database to identify the species present [1].
5: Advantages: it is rapid [1] and detects rare or hidden species without capturing them [1]. Limitations: it depends on complete reference databases [1]; it cannot easily estimate abundance and DNA may come from elsewhere or dead organisms [1].
6: A short, standard gene sequence that differs between species and is used to identify them.

title: A3.2 Classification and cladistics · Lesson 1 (HL): Why classify, the trouble with ranks, and clades
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.2 Classification and cladistics

tips: Number of species and what classification allows.

2.tip: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

1: There is an immense diversity of species, millions of them [1]; classification organises them so they can be identified, studied, predicted and communicated about [1].
2: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Birds evolved from reptiles (dinosaurs) and share a common ancestor with crocodiles [1], but are excluded from Reptilia, so the class does not include all descendants of its common ancestor [1].
3: Characteristics of members can be predicted because they are shared within the group [1]; it reflects evolutionary history/common ancestry, showing which organisms are most closely related [1].
4: Mammals and archosaurs are clades; “fish” without tetrapods leaves out descendants; flying animals share flight through convergence.
Similar morphology can arise by convergent evolution in unrelated groups [1]; sequence differences can be counted objectively and reflect time since divergence [1].
5: A clade is a group made of a common ancestor [1] and all of its descendants [1]; the most reliable evidence is base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins [1].
6: A group consisting of a common ancestor and all its descendants.

title: A3.2 Classification and cladistics · Lesson 2 (HL): Molecular clocks, building cladograms and reading them
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.2 Classification and cladistics

1: Mutation rates are not constant [1]; they vary with generation time, population size and selection pressure [1].
2: A and B (2 differences); D differs from all by 9, so it is the outgroup.
Root at the base; first node splits D from the rest; second node splits C from (A, B); third node splits A and B. Four terminal branches end in A, B, C, D.
3: Human and chimp share the most recent node; gorilla is their sister; orangutan branched first; all share the root ancestor.
A hypothetical common ancestor of the groups branching from it [1].
4: W–X 1, X–Y 1, Y–Z 2, W–Z 4 (W–Y 2, X–Z 3). Most parsimonious: Z (Y (W, X)) — W and X are closest, Y joins next, Z is the outgroup.
5: Sequences of the same gene are compared and differences counted [1]; organisms with fewer differences are more closely related and share a more recent common ancestor [1]; the cladogram requiring the fewest changes (parsimony) is chosen [1].
6: Choosing the cladogram that explains the data with the smallest number of sequence changes.

title: A3.2 Classification and cladistics · Lesson 3 (HL): Testing classifications with cladistics, and the three domains
summary: IB DP Biology · A3.2 Classification and cladistics

1: Cladistic analysis of gene sequences was carried out [1]; it showed the family was not a clade, its members coming from several separate lineages [1]; the shared flower structure was the result of convergent evolution, so genera were moved to other families [1].
2: Examples: “reptiles” excluding birds; vultures of the Old World and New World (look alike by convergence, different families); “fish” excluding tetrapods; elephant shrews (once grouped with true shrews).
3: E. coli and cyanobacteria: Bacteria; methanogens and halophiles: Archaea; yeast: Eukarya.
Base sequences of ribosomal RNA were compared [1]; they showed three distinct groups, with archaea as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes [1].
4: rRNA is present in all organisms [1] and evolves slowly, being highly conserved, so very distant groups can be compared [1].
5: Cladistics uses base or amino acid sequences to find evolutionary relationships [1]; when a traditional group is found not to be a clade (members not sharing a single common ancestor) [1], it is revised, e.g. figwort genera moved to other families because their similar flowers resulted from convergent evolution [1].

title: A4.1 Evolution and speciation · Lesson 1: Evolution and evidence from sequences and selective breeding
summary: IB DP Biology · A4.1 Evolution and speciation

1: Changes in allele or heritable trait frequency in populations are evolution; individual acquired changes are not.
2: Chimpanzee closest, horse intermediate, yeast most distant.
Species with more similar amino acid sequences in the same protein [1] share a more recent common ancestor, showing evolution from common ancestors [1].
3: Humans select individuals with desired traits for breeding [1]; the resulting breeds or varieties differ greatly from each other and from the wild ancestor [1]; this shows heritable change can happen rapidly, so natural selection over long periods could cause evolution [1].
4: Frog first (most differences), then horse, dog, rhesus monkey, and gorilla most recently.
5: Darwinian evolution is change in heritable (genetic) characteristics of a population [1]; Lamarckism wrongly proposed that characteristics acquired during an individual’s life are inherited [1].
6: Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations.

title: A4.1 Evolution and speciation · Lesson 2: Homologous and analogous structures, and speciation
summary: IB DP Biology · A4.1 Evolution and speciation

1: Tetrapod limbs share the same basic bone structure (one upper bone, two lower, wrist, five digits) [1] although used for different functions such as flying, swimming and running [1]; this suggests descent from a common ancestor with adaptive divergence [1].
2: Pentadactyl pairs are homologous; bird/insect wings and shark/dolphin fins are analogous.
3: New species form only by the splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more [1]; species do not arise from nothing, so splitting is the only source of new species [1].
4: The Congo River separated populations of an ancestral ape [1], preventing interbreeding/gene flow (geographical isolation) [1]; the populations faced different selection pressures, e.g. presence or absence of gorillas [1]; allele frequencies diverged until they became separate species [1].
5: Homologous structures share structure due to common ancestry [1], e.g. pentadactyl limbs of humans and bats [1]; analogous structures share function but have different origins (convergent evolution) [1], e.g. wings of birds and insects [1].

title: A4.1 Evolution and speciation · Lesson 3 (HL): Sympatric and allopatric speciation, adaptive radiation, hybrids and polyploidy
summary: IB DP Biology · A4.1 Evolution and speciation

1: Different months/times: temporal; mate preference: behavioural; rift: geographic.
2: One ancestral species diversifies into many species, each adapted to a different (vacant) niche [1]; because they use different niches they coexist without competing, increasing biodiversity [1].
3: Hybrids such as mules are sterile and cannot produce gametes [1], so alleles from one species cannot pass via the hybrid into the other species’ gene pool [1].
4: Two species hybridize, producing a usually sterile hybrid [1]; chromosome doubling makes it polyploid [1], so chromosomes can pair in meiosis and it is fertile, but it is reproductively isolated from both parents — a new species [1].
5: Both require reproductive isolation that stops gene flow [1]; in allopatric speciation populations are geographically separated [1]; in sympatric speciation they live in the same place, isolated by behaviour, timing or polyploidy [1].
6: Rapid evolution of one ancestral species into many species, each adapted to a different niche.

title: A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity · Lesson 1: Biodiversity, its history, extinctions and ecosystem loss
summary: IB DP Biology · A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity

tips: What has not been found, and why?

1: Coat patterns and rice varieties: genetic; bird species: species; habitat range: ecosystem.
2: Many species have not yet been discovered or described [1], especially small organisms such as insects, fungi and microbes, or those in remote habitats like the deep sea [1].
3: Moas were overhunted by human settlers [1]; they were large, flightless, slow-breeding and had evolved without mammalian predators so did not avoid humans [1]; forest burning also destroyed their habitat [1].
Moa: overhunting; monk seal: hunting plus overfishing of prey; cichlids: invasive Nile perch.
4: Logging of dipterocarp trees for hardwood timber [1]; clearance for oil palm plantations and other agriculture [1].
5: The North Island giant moa [1] was driven extinct by overhunting by human settlers [1]; Lake Victoria cichlids / the Caribbean monk seal [1] were lost to an invasive predator (Nile perch) / hunting combined with overfishing of prey [1].
6: Ecosystem diversity, species diversity and genetic diversity.

title: A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity · Lesson 2: The biodiversity crisis, its causes and conservation
summary: IB DP Biology · A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity

tips: Where, plus an advantage of each.

1: A single survey gives a snapshot; repeated surveys show change over time [1], provided they use the same sites and methods so results are comparable [1].
Coverage and engagement are benefits; misidentification and uneven effort are concerns.
2: Poaching: over-exploitation; tea: habitat loss; pesticides: pollution; hyacinth: invasive species.
3: Sanctuary: in situ; zoos: ex situ; beavers: rewilding; frozen seeds: seed bank.

In situ conserves species in their natural habitat, also protecting their ecosystem and interactions [1]; ex situ conserves them outside it, in zoos, botanic gardens or seed banks [1]; ex situ protects species from immediate threats and allows breeding for reintroduction, but populations may be small with low genetic diversity [1].
4: They are evolutionarily distinct, with few close relatives, so their loss removes unique evolutionary history and genetic diversity [1]; they are globally endangered, so action is urgent [1].
5: No single approach is sufficient, as species and threats differ [1]; in situ protection conserves habitats and ecosystems [1]; ex situ measures such as zoos and seed banks safeguard species too threatened to survive in the wild and provide backup for reintroduction [1].

title: B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids · Lesson 1: Carbon, condensation and hydrolysis
summary: IB DP Biology · B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids

tips: Name the reaction, product and bond.
One similarity and the key difference.

1: Each carbon atom can form four bonds [1]; these are strong covalent bonds with carbon and other non-metal atoms, single or double [1]; so carbon can form chains, branches and rings of many sizes [1].
2: By a condensation reaction [1], in which a molecule of water is removed (–OH from one, –H from the other) [1] and a peptide bond forms between the amino acids [1].
3: Water is used [1], and the water molecule is split to provide –H and –OH groups as the glycosidic bond breaks, releasing glucose/maltose [1].
Building is condensation; digestion is hydrolysis.
4: Making a chain of five glucose units released four water molecules (one per bond); hydrolysing it back to five monomers used four water molecules.
5: Both involve covalent bonds between monomers and are catalysed by enzymes [1]; condensation joins monomers and releases water [1]; hydrolysis breaks the bond by adding and splitting water [1].
6: Nine — one for each glycosidic bond.

title: B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids · Lesson 2: Monosaccharides, polysaccharides and glycoproteins
summary: IB DP Biology · B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids

1: Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses; glucose and fructose are hexoses.
Glucose is soluble in water because of its polar –OH groups, so it is easily transported in plasma [1]; it releases energy when oxidised in respiration [1].
2: It is highly branched, so it is compact [1]; it is large and insoluble, so it does not affect osmosis or leave the cell [1]; the many branch ends allow glucose to be added or removed quickly [1].
3: Cellulose is made of beta-glucose [1] whose alternating orientation gives straight chains [1]; parallel chains are cross-linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils with high tensile strength [1].
4: Glycoproteins carry specific carbohydrate chains [1] on the outer surface of the membrane, which other cells or antibodies recognise [1]; e.g. group A red cells carry A antigens, which are recognised as foreign by anti-A antibodies in group B or O people [1].
5: Both are polysaccharides of glucose joined by glycosidic bonds [1]; starch is made of alpha-glucose [1], cellulose of beta-glucose [1]; starch chains coil/branch, while cellulose chains are straight and cross-linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils [1].
6: We lack the enzyme cellulase that hydrolyses the beta-glycosidic bonds between beta-glucose units.

title: B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids · Lesson 3: Lipids, triglycerides and fatty acids
summary: IB DP Biology · B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids

1: Butter fat; sunflower oil; cuticle wax; cholesterol steroid.
2: 1 glycerol, 3 fatty acids, 3 waters; phospholipid has 2 fatty acids.
One glycerol molecule [1] combines with three fatty acids [1] by condensation reactions that release three water molecules and form ester bonds [1].
3: Plant oils contain mostly unsaturated fatty acids with C=C double bonds [1], which create kinks so the chains cannot pack closely [1], giving lower melting points; saturated animal fats have straight chains and higher melting points [1].
4: Lipids dissolve in ethanol (non-polar solvent) but not in water; when the ethanol solution is poured into water the lipid comes out of solution as tiny droplets, forming the cloudy emulsion.
5: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds [1]; unsaturated have one or more C=C double bonds [1]; so unsaturated chains are kinked and have lower melting points, while saturated are straight with higher melting points [1].

title: B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids · Lesson 4: Adipose tissue, phospholipid bilayers and steroids
summary: IB DP Biology · B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids

tips: Fat as an insulator in a hot habitat.

1: Fat releases about twice as much energy per gram as glycogen [1] because it has more oxidisable hydrogen/carbon and less oxygen [1]; it is insoluble and stored without water, so stores are lighter [1].
Fat is a thermal insulator [1]; concentrating it in a hump leaves the rest of the body able to lose heat, avoiding overheating in the hot desert [1].
2: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails [1]; heads face the water and tails face inward away from the water, forming a bilayer [1].
3: Testosterone is a non-polar steroid [1], so it diffuses directly through the phospholipid bilayer into the cell [1].
The four-ring compound and oestradiol are steroids; a triglyceride and the protein insulin are not.
4: 740 ÷ 37 = 20 g lipid; 740 ÷ 17 = 43.5 g carbohydrate (and glycogen is stored with water, so even heavier).
5: Long-term energy storage in adipose tissue [1]; thermal insulation, reducing heat loss in cold habitats [1].
6: They are non-polar, so they diffuse through the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer.

title: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport · Lesson 1: Lipid bilayers, simple diffusion and membrane proteins
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

tips: Name the process, the gradient and the route.
Compare the two particles and the core.

1: Phospholipids are amphipathic: the phosphate heads are hydrophilic [1] and the hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic [1]; so in water the heads face the water on both sides and the tails face each other inside, away from the water [1].
2: O₂ and CO₂ are small and non-polar, so they cross; ions, glucose and proteins do not.
3: By simple diffusion [1]: oxygen is used in respiration, so its concentration is lower inside than outside, creating a concentration gradient [1]; O₂ is small and non-polar so it passes between the phospholipids [1].
4: Channels and pumps are integral (transmembrane); surface-attached proteins are peripheral.
Integral proteins are embedded in one or both layers of the bilayer (often spanning it) [1]; peripheral proteins are attached to one surface, not embedded [1].
5: O₂ is small and non-polar, so it passes between the phospholipids [1]; K⁺ is charged (hydrophilic) [1] and cannot pass through the hydrophobic hydrocarbon core of the bilayer [1].
6: It has a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails.

title: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport · Lesson 2: Osmosis, aquaporins, channels and pumps
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

1: The cytoplasm has a higher solute concentration than distilled water [1]; the membrane is impermeable to these solutes [1]; so there is a net movement of water into the cell by osmosis (random movement, more water crossing inward) [1].
2: The protein forms a hydrophilic pore through the membrane [1]; its diameter and the charges lining it allow only a specific ion to pass [1]; gated channels let ions through only when open [1].
No ATP; down the gradient; needs a channel or carrier protein.
3: By active transport [1]: pump proteins in the membrane bind nitrate ions and move them into the cell [1] using energy from ATP, which allows movement against the concentration gradient [1].
4: CO₂ simple diffusion; K⁺ facilitated diffusion; water osmosis; Na⁺ active transport.
5: Both use specific membrane proteins, so both are selective [1]; facilitated diffusion moves particles down the concentration gradient (passive) [1]; active transport can move them against the gradient [1] using energy from ATP [1].
6: Facilitated diffusion (channels) and active transport (pumps), because each protein transports only specific particles.

title: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport · Lesson 3: Glycoproteins, glycolipids and the fluid mosaic model
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

1: Cell recognition, e.g. acting as antigens that identify cells as self or as a blood group [1]; cell adhesion, binding cells together to form tissues [1].
Carbohydrates outside; tails in the core; cytoskeleton-linked peripheral proteins inside.
2: Fluid: phospholipids and proteins can move sideways within the layer, so the membrane is flexible [1]; mosaic: proteins are scattered through the bilayer like tiles of a mosaic [1].
3: Labels: phospholipid bilayer, hydrophilic phosphate head, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail, integral (transmembrane) protein, peripheral protein, glycoprotein, carbohydrate chain, cholesterol, hydrophilic region, hydrophobic region. The side with the carbohydrate chains is extracellular.
Carbohydrates only outside; heads face outward; cholesterol between tails and spanning proteins are correct.
4: When a mouse cell and a human cell with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused [1], the labels became evenly mixed over the hybrid cell surface within about 40 minutes, so proteins must move sideways [1].
5: A phospholipid bilayer [1] with hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous solutions on both sides [1] and hydrophobic tails forming the core [1]; integral and peripheral proteins, glycoproteins and cholesterol are embedded or attached [1].
6: The extracellular side; cell recognition and cell adhesion.

title: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport · Lesson 4 (HL): Membrane fluidity, cholesterol and vesicles
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

3.tip: Into or out of the cell?

tips: What must the vesicle membrane do?

1: Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds that kink the chains [1], so they pack loosely and have lower melting points [1]; the membrane therefore stays fluid and flexible at low temperatures instead of becoming rigid [1].
Hot spring bacteria: saturated; Antarctic fish and reindeer legs: unsaturated.
2: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids with its –OH near the heads [1]; at high temperatures it restricts phospholipid movement, stabilising the membrane [1]; at low temperatures it prevents tight packing so the membrane does not stiffen [1].
3: Engulfing and taking in fluid are endocytosis; releasing enzyme and neurotransmitter are exocytosis.
The vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane [1]; this is possible because both are fluid bilayers whose phospholipids can move and rearrange, so they merge without tearing [1].
4: At low temperature more unsaturated fatty acids keep the membrane fluid [1]; at high temperature more saturated fatty acids keep the membrane stable and not too fluid/leaky [1].
5: The plasma membrane folds inward around material [1] and pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell [1], e.g. phagocytosis of bacteria by a macrophage [1].
6: At high temperatures it reduces fluidity (stabilises); at low temperatures it prevents stiffening.

title: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport · Lesson 5 (HL): Gated channels, the sodium–potassium pump, cotransport and cell adhesion
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport

tips: Where does the energy come from?

1: The acetylcholine receptor is ligand (neurotransmitter)-gated; axonal Na⁺ and K⁺ channels are voltage-gated.
2: It pumps three Na⁺ out [1] for every two K⁺ in [1] using energy from ATP, so more positive charge leaves the cell, making the inside negative and setting up concentration gradients [1].
3: The cotransporter uses the energy of Na⁺ diffusing in down its gradient [1]; this gradient is created by Na⁺/K⁺ pumps that use ATP [1]; so glucose is moved against its own concentration gradient without direct use of ATP [1].
Pump uses ATP; SGLT moves Na⁺ with glucose; aquaporins let water pass.
4: CAMs are membrane proteins that bind cells to each other or to the extracellular matrix [1], forming junctions that hold cells together in tissues [1].
5: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps use ATP [1] to keep the Na⁺ concentration low inside the cells [1]; Na⁺ diffuses in from the lumen through sodium–glucose cotransporters, carrying glucose with it [1], even against glucose’s concentration gradient (indirect active transport) [1].
6: Three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in.

title: B2.3 Cell specialization · Lesson 1: Differentiation, stem cells and stem cell niches
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.3 Cell specialization

1: Signalling chemicals form concentration gradients across the embryo [1]; cells at different positions receive different concentrations, which switch on different genes [1], so they differentiate into different cell types [1].
2: Repeated division and multiple pathways are stem cell properties.
3: Niches maintain stem cells and control when they proliferate and differentiate [1]; e.g. bone marrow produces blood cells [1]; hair follicles regenerate hair and repair skin [1].
4: Benefit: they can differentiate into any cell type, potentially treating diseases such as diabetes or spinal injury. Concern: obtaining them destroys an early embryo, which some believe has moral status; risk of tumours.
5: Different genes are expressed (switched on) in different cells [1], producing different proteins, so cells develop different structures and functions (differentiation) [1].
6: It can divide endlessly and differentiate along different pathways.

title: B2.3 Cell specialization · Lesson 2: Types of stem cell, cell size and surface area-to-volume ratio
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.3 Cell specialization

1: Zygote and 4-cell embryo totipotent; inner cell mass pluripotent; bone marrow multipotent.
2: RBC 7 µm; egg 100 µm; neuron up to 1 m; muscle fibre several cm.
3: As a cell grows its volume increases faster than its surface area [1], so the SA:V ratio decreases [1]; the surface cannot exchange materials fast enough to meet the needs of the larger volume, and diffusion distances become too long [1].
4: Small cubes decolourise fastest because they have the largest SA:V and shortest distance to the centre; the 3 cm cube takes longest, showing why large cells exchange less efficiently.
5: Totipotent cells can form any cell type including extra-embryonic tissues/whole organism [1]; pluripotent cells can form any body cell type but not a whole organism or placenta [1].

title: B2.3 Cell specialization · Lesson 3 (HL): Specialized cells: SA:V adaptations, pneumocytes, muscle and gametes
summary: IB DP Biology · B2.3 Cell specialization

tips: Two for type I, one for type II.

2: Thin and diffusion: type I; lamellar bodies and surfactant: type II.
3: Myofibrils both; branched and intercalated discs cardiac; multinucleate and long skeletal.
Fibres are formed by fusion of many cells and are very long [1]; many nuclei are needed to control and supply proteins (e.g. actin, myosin) throughout the large cell [1].

Blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is pumped again [1], so it reaches body tissues at high pressure, delivering oxygen faster to support high metabolic rates [1].

It shows a (negative) correlation between light and moss cover [1], but does not prove causation, because another factor that varies with light, such as soil moisture or humidity, could be responsible [1].

2: Cyanobacteria and maize use light (photoautotrophs); iron and nitrifying bacteria use oxidation of inorganic chemicals (chemoautotrophs); yeast uses sugars made by other organisms (heterotroph).
Energy is needed to fix carbon dioxide into organic compounds [1] and to drive the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules such as proteins and polysaccharides [1].
3: Plant proteins are digested (hydrolysed by proteases) in the gut [1] into amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood [1]; they are then assimilated: joined by condensation on ribosomes into the goat’s own proteins [1].
Digestion breaks down; absorption takes in; assimilation builds the body’s own molecules.
4: Plants respire as well as photosynthesise; all organisms respire [1], plants doing so in all living cells day and night to produce ATP [1].
All three oxidise carbon compounds in aerobic cell respiration to release energy for ATP, producing CO₂ as a waste product.
5: Both make their own carbon compounds from inorganic substances such as CO₂ [1]; photoautotrophs use light energy [1]; chemoautotrophs use energy from oxidising inorganic chemicals, e.g. iron-oxidising bacteria [1].

Decomposers feed on dead organic matter such as faeces and dead organisms [1]; they digest it and release its energy in respiration [1]; this returns mineral nutrients to the soil for producers, recycling them [1].
6: An autotroph makes its own carbon compounds from inorganic substances using light or chemical energy; a heterotroph obtains carbon compounds from other organisms.

Both carry out cell respiration, making ATP and then using it [1]; energy transfers are not 100% efficient, so some energy is converted to heat each time [1].
4: Energy is lost at every transfer, so only about 10% passes on [1]; losses are mainly heat from respiration, plus uneaten and undigested material [1]; after four or five levels too little energy remains to sustain another population [1].
Total biomass falls; energy per gram does not; top predator populations are small.
5: 2 100 ÷ 24 000 × 100 = 8.75% [1]. The producers use much of the energy in their own respiration, lost as heat [1]; much plant material is not eaten [1]; uneaten dead plant matter and herbivore faeces pass to decomposers [1].
6: Energy is lost as heat from respiration at each level, and some material is not eaten or not digested, so each level receives less energy than the one below.

title: C4.2 Transfers of energy and matter · Lesson 4: Primary and secondary production, and the carbon cycle

Rainforest highest, savanna middle, desert lowest.
2: Heterotrophs convert much of the carbon compounds they eat into CO₂ and water in respiration [1], so this carbon is lost from biomass [1]; also not all producer biomass is eaten or digested [1].
3: Atmosphere → producers: photosynthesis; producers → consumers: feeding; producers, consumers, decomposers → atmosphere: respiration; producers/consumers → dead organic matter: death and egestion; dead organic matter → atmosphere: decomposer respiration; fossil fuels → atmosphere: combustion.
Photosynthesis, feeding, respiration and combustion respectively.
4: Waterlogged peat is anaerobic, so decomposition is slow and photosynthesis exceeds respiration [1]; draining lets oxygen in, so decomposers respire the peat rapidly [1]; respiration then exceeds photosynthesis, giving a net release of CO₂ [1].
5: Primary production is accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs [1]; secondary production is accumulation in biomass by heterotrophs [1].
The trees take in CO₂ by photosynthesis [1] faster than it is released by respiration, so carbon accumulates in wood and other biomass (net uptake) [1].
6: Photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so there is a net uptake of CO₂ and carbon accumulates in biomass or peat.

Dead organic matter would accumulate without being broken down [1]; minerals such as nitrate and phosphate would not be returned to the soil, so plant growth would decline [1].

4: There are 20 amino acids to code for [1]; a doublet code gives only 16 combinations, while a triplet gives 64, enough for all [1].

Binding, scanning, initiator tRNA, large subunit.

title: D1.3 Mutation and gene editing · Lesson 1: Types of gene mutation and their consequences
summary: IB DP Biology · D1.3 Mutation and gene editing

The genetic code is degenerate, with several codons for most amino acids [1], so the new codon may code for the same amino acid (silent/same-sense) [1].
3: A deletion shifts the reading frame (frameshift) [1], changing every codon after the mutation and therefore many amino acids, often creating a stop codon [1]; a substitution changes at most one codon/amino acid [1].

title: D2.1 Cell and nuclear division · Lesson 2: Replication, chromosome condensation and the phases of mitosis

DNA is replicated so each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids [1]; in anaphase the chromatids separate to opposite poles [1]; so each pole/nucleus receives one copy of every chromosome [1].

3: Calluna heath: pioneer heather → building → mature → degenerate phase, when old plants collapse leaving gaps colonised by lichens and mosses, then new heather seedlings start the cycle again. Or savanna: grassland → woodland as trees grow → fire and elephants open it back to grassland.

title: D4.3 Climate change · Lesson 1: Causes of climate change, positive feedbacks, boreal tipping points and polar ice
summary: IB DP Biology · D4.3 Climate change

1: Combustion and deforestation: CO₂; cattle and rice: methane.
2: Ice reflects most sunlight (high albedo) [1]; when it melts the darker ocean absorbs more solar radiation [1], warming further and melting more ice, amplifying warming [1].
3: Warmer temperatures and less snowfall cause drought [1], reducing photosynthesis and primary production and causing forest browning [1]; fires and decomposition then release more carbon than is fixed, a net loss [1].
4: Emperor penguin on landfast ice; walrus on Arctic sea ice.
5: Loss of reflective snow and ice [1] means more solar radiation is absorbed, causing more warming [1]; warming thaws permafrost/accelerates decomposition/warms oceans [1], releasing more CO₂ and methane [1].

title: D4.3 Climate change · Lesson 2: Ocean upwelling, range shifts, coral reefs and carbon sequestration
summary: IB DP Biology · D4.3 Climate change

1: Warm surface water prevents upwelling of cold deep water [1], so fewer nutrients reach the surface [1]; phytoplankton production falls, reducing energy flow up the food chain to fish [1].
2: Species move upslope to stay within their temperature tolerance [1], but at the summit there is no higher land, and the area available shrinks, so they may go extinct [1].

4: Fast growth and timber: plantation; biodiversity and resilience: native.
5: Fast-growing non-native trees take up carbon quickly [1]; but plantations are monocultures with low biodiversity and may use a lot of water [1]; native forest regeneration supports more biodiversity and resilience, though it stores carbon more slowly [1].
6: High water temperatures causing corals to expel their zooxanthellae.

title: D4.3 Climate change · Lesson 3 (HL): Phenology, mismatched timing, insect life cycles and evolution
